abstract: Biomolecular condensates are essential to cellular processes and organization, and are typically formed by weak, multivalent interactions among biomolecules, such as intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Because condensates are much more viscous than the surrounding solution, they are generally expected to slow protein motions. While the length-scale-dependent dynamics of IDPs in dilute and dense phases have been studied separately, a systematic comparison of how these dynamics change upon phase separation remains lacking. In this study, we use coarse-grained, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations to compare the segmental dynamics between the dilute and dense phases of the low-complexity domain of the RNA-binding protein Fused in Sarcoma (FUS-LC) and compositionally similar model IDPs of different lengths. Short protein segments, contrary to expectation, relax faster within the condensate than in the dilute phase, whereas segments longer than about one-seventh of the chain relax more slowly. Our results suggest that this crossover arises because chain collapse in the dilute phase slows local relaxation, whereas neighboring chains in the condensate slow chain-scale relaxation. The dilute phase sets both the magnitude of the speed-up and the segment length up to which it extends: dilute-phase relaxation changes with chain length and interaction strength, whereas relaxation within the condensate, at a fixed protein concentration, does not. Slower water dynamics increase the speed-up, whereas removing water eliminates it. Overall, our results suggest that condensates slow global protein motions but accelerate local ones, which may help preserve the liquid-like nature of the condensate's interior.
